facts.claim: "The Preacher" is the closing track (track 6, 3:40) of Jamie N Commons' Rumble and Sway EP, released on KIDinaKORNER/Interscope.
Jamie N Commons is the sole credited songwriter of "The Preacher".
An AllMusic-sourced review describes the track as Rick Rubin-produced, with a spoken-word, Internet-themed 'promo' spot in the middle.
The song first appeared on Commons' debut EP The Baron (2011, Luv Luv Luv Records), and the Rumble and Sway EP, produced by Alex da Kid, followed in early 2013.
The lyrics tell of a Southern pastor who strangles his wife and dismembers her body.
One blog describes the narrator as an evangelical preacher from Alabama who strangled his wife and put her chopped-up body in a freezer.

Commons said the follow-up video for 'Devil In Me' was made by the same directors, James Willis and Ben Murray, who made the first video for 'The Preacher'. Its start includes the instrumental section of 'The Preacher' playing on a record player.

Commons has said he wants to 'push the boundaries of what blues can be' and make the sound accessible to people who don't normally listen to blues. In 2012 he was heading to the US to meet producer Rick Rubin.
The song has been used in TV, including Justified (S6E7, 2015) and Tidelands (S1E6, 2018).
Commons was born in Bristol and moved to Chicago at age six, where he absorbed Chicago blues. He later moved to London and studied music at Goldsmiths.

research.lineage: Commons' gravel-voiced 'modern gothic' blues, with murder-ballad storytelling, draws comparisons to Tom Waits and Nick Cave and to the Chicago blues and Southern swamp-gospel tradition.

draft:
The hinge of **The Preacher** is a single swapped line. Early on, someone cries "Oh Lord what have you done," a voice of horror telling the condemned man he'll never see heaven. By the end the words have been rewritten, and the cry is a demand: "Now show me heaven or kingdom come." Same melody, same refrain, but the man on the gallows has stopped asking forgiveness and started presenting an invoice.

Jamie N Commons wrote it alone, and he tells it as a murder ballad, the old form where the killing is already done and the song lives in its aftermath. Accounts of the song describe a preacher who strangled his wife. The lyric never says so outright. It circles the act through what's left behind: "the blood turning dry on his hands," and a refrain that tallies the damage like a ledger, Jesus and his family named as "two things he's lost." The central image does the rest. "One hand on the trigger, one hand on the cross" is a man holding his violence and his faith at the same time and refusing to let go of either.

The song's most unsettling move is letting him speak. Halfway through, the narration hands over the floor, and the preacher addresses his "wayward flock" with a noose around his neck. His defense is plain: "His bidding was all I could do." He doesn't sound like a man hiding guilt. He sounds certain, and the certainty is the horror. Commons also doesn't let the crowd off. The mob calling for the scaffold has "blood in their eyes and blood in their hearts," so the righteousness on both sides of the rope starts to look alike. The song never settles whether the preacher is mad or damned or simply believes what he says. It leaves you standing in the square with everyone else.

The band plays it straight and steady, which suits a hanging. Strummed acoustic guitar and a simple bass line sit on a kick-and-snare beat that drives forward without hurrying. An electric guitar adds long, sustained notes above it. The room sounds like a real one, with some natural reverb and a raw edge. Commons sings in a gravelly, weathered voice with the deliberate pacing of someone telling a story at the edge of a fire.

That gothic blues has drawn comparisons to Tom Waits and Nick Cave, and the roots go back further. Commons was born in Bristol, moved to Chicago at six and absorbed the city's blues there. He has said he wants to "push the boundaries of what blues can be" for listeners who don't usually go near it. The song first appeared on his 2011 debut EP, The Baron, and returned as the closing track of Rumble and Sway. It later scored a scene of *Justified*, a show that knows a thing or two about men who mistake their own will for God's.

What sticks is how reasonable the preacher sounds, and how close the song lets you get to a conviction you'd never want to share.

factCheck.claim: The hinge is a single swapped line; early on someone cries 'Oh Lord what have you done,' a voice of horror telling the condemned man he'll never see heaven
factCheck.note: The lyrics attribute both cries to 'He cries', so a separate horrified voice isn't supported. It's also two lines that change, not one. Rewritten as the same refrain turning from dismay with heaven ruled out into a demand. The first quote was dropped to stay within the three-line quote limit.
